terms.definition: Your pay before any taxes or deductions come out, for one paycheck or for the year.
What actually lands in your bank account on payday, after taxes and deductions are taken out.
The fixed yearly pay in your offer letter, before bonuses, overtime, or anything taken out.
How often you are paid; biweekly means every two weeks, which is 26 paychecks in most years.
The statement that comes with each paycheck and lists your gross pay, each tax and deduction, and your net pay, for that check and for the year so far.
The total so far this calendar year, as a pay stub shows it, such as your earnings or the tax withheld since January 1.
An amount taken out of your gross pay for something you signed up for, such as a health premium or a 401(k) contribution.
A deduction taken out before income tax is figured, so it lowers the pay you are taxed on; traditional 401(k) contributions and most health premiums work this way.
A deduction taken out after taxes are figured, so it does not lower your tax now; Roth 401(k) contributions and ESPP purchases work this way.
The pay left after pre-tax deductions, which is the amount income tax is figured on.
Income tax your employer takes out of each paycheck and sends to the government for you, as a prepayment on what you owe for the year.
The IRS form you fill out when you start a job, which tells your employer how much federal income tax to withhold.
The category you file your tax return under, such as single or married filing jointly, which sets your tax brackets and standard deduction.
A range of income taxed at one rate; your marginal rate is the rate on your last dollar, and moving into a higher bracket raises the tax only on the income inside it.
Social Security and Medicare taxes together, taken out of almost every paycheck at fixed rates and matched by your employer.
The part of FICA that funds retirement and disability benefits, charged on your wages up to a yearly limit.
The part of FICA that funds health coverage for people 65 and older, charged on all your wages with no yearly limit.
Colorado taxes income at a single flat rate, and your employer withholds it from each paycheck along with federal income tax.

Colorado's Family and Medical Leave Insurance program, paid for by a small premium split between you and your employer, which pays part of your wages while you are on leave for a new child, a serious illness, or caring for family.
A flat monthly tax that a few Colorado cities, such as Denver and Aurora, charge people who work there, with part paid by you and part by your employer.
What you pay each paycheck to have a health, dental, or other insurance plan, whether or not you use it.
The amount you pay for covered care each year before the plan starts paying its share.
Your share of a covered bill after you have met the deductible, as a percentage, such as 20%.
A fixed amount you pay for a doctor visit or a prescription, with the plan paying the rest.
The most you pay for covered care in one plan year, not counting premiums; after you reach it, the plan pays all covered costs.
Who a plan covers, such as you alone, you and a spouse, or your whole family, which sets how much the premium is.
Doctors and hospitals that have agreed prices with your plan, so care from them costs you less than care out of network.
A health plan with a higher premium and a lower deductible that lets you see doctors in or out of its network, paying less in network.
A health plan with a lower premium and a higher deductible, and the only kind of plan that lets you put money in an HSA.
A savings account you can have with an HDHP, where money goes in before tax, grows tax-free, and comes out tax-free for medical costs, and it stays yours if you change jobs.
Money your employer puts into your HSA each year, on top of what you put in yourself.
An account you fund from your paycheck before tax to pay medical costs during the plan year, where money you do not spend by the deadline is mostly lost.
The twelve months a benefits choice covers, often January to December, with its own deductible and out-of-pocket maximum.
A retirement savings account through your employer, funded straight from your paycheck, where the money grows without tax until you take it out in retirement.
The after-tax kind of 401(k): you pay tax on the money now, and it comes out tax-free in retirement.
A retirement account you open yourself, outside work, with after-tax money that comes out tax-free in retirement, and with a yearly limit and an income limit.
Money your employer adds to your 401(k) when you contribute, up to a limit, such as 100% of what you put in up to 6% of your pay.
When money your employer put into your account becomes yours to keep if you leave the job; your own contributions are always yours.
The most the IRS lets you put into an account such as a 401(k), HSA, or IRA in one year; the amounts change each year.
Savings set aside for surprises such as a job loss or a car repair, often three to six months of expenses, kept where you can reach it quickly.
A plan that lets you buy your employer's stock through paycheck deductions, usually at a discount.
How far below the market price you pay for ESPP shares, such as 15%.
The stretch of time, often six months, during which your ESPP deductions build up before shares are bought for you.
An ESPP feature that bases your price on the lower of the stock's price at the start or the end of the offering period, then takes the discount off that.
How long you must, or choose to, keep ESPP shares before selling them, which affects both your risk and your taxes.
The risk of having too much of your money in one company, which is worse when it is your employer, since one bad year could cost you your job and your savings at once.
The yearly window, often in November, when you can change your benefits for the next plan year.
The last day to choose your benefits as a new hire; if you miss it, you may be left with default or no coverage until the next open enrollment.
A change such as marriage, a new child, or losing other coverage that lets you change your benefits outside open enrollment.
